To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
obese and lean Zucker rats self-select their diet in such a way as to maintain a high intake of fat.

1) obese Zucker rats do not consume more fat than lean Zucker rats when given access to a fat source, 2) obese and lean rats consume more fat than they did before the fat source was diluted, 3) the increased fat consumption was not simply compensational in nature,
obese Zucker rats are not genetically programmed to over-consume fat.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of dietary fat dilutions on the intake of lean and obese rats and the implications of these results on the regulation of body weight.
the effects of dietary fat dilutions on the food intake and body composition of the obese Zucker rat and the lean rat.
the development of new approaches to understanding the mechanisms of obesity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the obese Zucker rat has the ability to self-select a diet that is high in fat and low in protein, and this diet promotes the development and maintenance of its obesity.
obese Zucker rats do not differ from their lean littermates in their ability to select their diets.
obese rats do not eat more fat than lean rats, but that both lean and obese eat as much fat as they want when they have a choice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
obese Zucker rats are not unique in their preference for dietary fat, but rather they are unique in their ability to consume more dietary fat.
the obese rat does not eat more than the lean rat because it wants to eat more, but because it has a different set of internal controls that allow it to eat more.
the obese rat is a model for the human obese, and that both are characterized by a lack of precision in caloric regulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the obese Zucker rat does not appear to be a unique animal model of obesity.
self-selection of dietary macronutrients can be a powerful tool for understanding the regulation of food intake and body weight in animals and humans.
the obese Zucker rat is not a model of obesity.
